column4: The section's root gloss for خ ل ق contrasts true making with fabricated claims; this verse says God خلق the human and fashioned him, grounding 95:4's human creation in an explicit account of proportioning.
The section's 95:4 image is a human made in excellent form; this next verse says God assembled the person in whatever صورة He willed, giving the concrete bodily form that 82:7 introduces.

The section asks how anyone can deny the dīn after God made the human; this immediate continuation says بل تكذبون بالدين, placing denial of recompense directly after the creation and fashioning in 82:7–8.

The section defines amānah as the opposite of betrayal and ends with God as الحكم; this verse commands that trusts be returned to their owners and that people be judged justly, joining those two claims in one command from God.

The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن includes trusting someone in judgment, while its gloss for ء م ن makes faith assent; here true belief requires making the Messenger judge and inwardly accepting his ruling without resistance.

The section's gloss for د ي ن connects trust with judgment; here people called to Allah and the Messenger for judgment turn away, a concrete refusal of the trustworthy ruling the section sets against assent.
The section contrasts accepting a word with rejecting its speaker; this continuation says they come submissively when the ruling favors them, exposing selective rather than settled acceptance.
The section describes doubt as a heart that wanders; this question names disease, doubt, and fear of injustice as reasons for refusing judgment, completing the scene begun in 24:48.
The section's iman gloss is tasdīq, accepting a true word; the believers' answer here is “we hear and obey” when summoned for judgment, the settled response opposite to the turning away in 24:48.
The section joins faith, good action, and lasting reward; this continuation associates obedience to Allah and His Messenger, fear of God, and piety with success, explaining the stance shown in 24:51.

The section uses Yusuf's brothers' claim in 12:17 to show how belief can be withheld; two verses earlier they ask why Jacob does not trust them with Yusuf (لَا تَأْمَنَّا), setting up the very trust their actions betray.

The brothers promise to guard Yusuf and say he will enjoy himself; this assurance is the specific speech that their later act and wolf story falsify, making the section's trust-versus-lying-in-deed distinction concrete.
Jacob says Yusuf's going away will grieve him and fears a wolf may eat him while they are unaware; the next events show his fear was warranted and expose the brothers' confident promise as false.
The brothers answer Jacob that their strong group would be losers if a wolf ate Yusuf; their own group abandons him, so the verse records a confident assurance contradicted by the deed.
After promising protection, the brothers put Yusuf in the bottom of a well; this betrayal is the acted falsehood that the section says can accompany lying in speech.

The brothers return at night weeping after the betrayal; their performed grief adds a false outward display to the false account that follows, matching the section's point that a state or action can lie.

The section explicitly cites the brothers' words ما أنت بمؤمن لنا ولو كنا صادقين: they pre-empt belief in their report even while claiming truth, and then blame the wolf, staging the conflict between trust and false testimony.

The section's dictionary entry for ك ذ ب calls a dyed cloth that looks embroidered a garment that “lies by its state”; here the brothers stain Yusuf's shirt with false blood as proof of their fabricated wolf story.

The section's secondary gloss calls deceptive cloth a surface that misstates what happened; in this later Yusuf scene, his answer to the adultery charge is tested by the shirt's tear, so the garment can expose rather than conceal a lie.

This witness says that a shirt torn from behind would show that the woman lied and Yusuf spoke truth; the shirt's physical state distinguishes the competing claims, a precise reversal of the section's deceptive-cloth image.

When the husband sees the shirt torn from behind, he calls the accusation a plot; the fabric here tells the truth about the action, countering the section's dictionary example of fabric that lies by appearance.

The section labels the root ء م ن's iman sense as tasdīq and links security to a settled heart; this verse corrects people who say “we believe”: faith has not entered their hearts, so their spoken claim is not yet inward assent.

After distinguishing mere profession in 49:14, this verse describes true believers as those who believe and then do not doubt; that untroubled heart directly answers the section's picture of trust as calmness.

The section's root gloss for ء م ن treats believing as affirming a true word; these people say they believe in God and the Last Day, while the verse says they are not believers, a direct boundary between speech and inward truth.

The section says a word may lie in speech and deed; these speakers claim faith while trying to deceive God and believers, though the verse says they deceive only themselves, completing the false profession in 2:8.
The section locates trust in the heart's stillness; this continuation describes disease in the hearts of those who falsely profess belief, making their inward disorder the opposite of that stillness.

The section distinguishes accepting truth from merely saying words; this verse describes people whose mouths say “we believe” while their hearts do not, and who listen eagerly to lies, joining false profession to false report.

The section says trust depends on truthful speech and a reliable speaker; the hypocrites testify that Muhammad is God's Messenger, but God calls them liars, separating a true sentence from the speaker's false stance.
The section says a lie can be an act as well as a statement; these speakers use their oaths as a shield and turn people from God's way, giving their false testimony a deceptive function.
The section explicitly says lying is said of both speech and action; this address asks believers why they say what they do not do, naming the same gap between words and deeds.
This continuation says God greatly detests saying what one does not do; it supplies the judgment on the speech/action mismatch named in 61:2 and in the section's dictionary note.
The section says a lie can occur in word and act; these people say “obedience” to the Messenger, then privately plan otherwise, a direct case of speech contradicted by deed.
The section defines amānah against betrayal; this warning names betrayal of God, the Messenger, and one's trusts as a knowing act, giving the opposite boundary of the reliable person.
The section's word emīn means a trustworthy person; this description of successful believers says they keep their trusts and covenants, showing trustworthiness in conduct rather than only a title.
This repeated formulation says believers preserve their trusts and pledges; it concretely echoes the section's amānah/emīn link and binds reliability to their other acts of worship.
The section's 95:6 joins belief with righteous action; this account of righteousness includes belief and fulfilling a promise when made, making reliable action part of what genuine faith looks like.

The section links the ء م ن root in faith with the removal of fear; this verse promises security to those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing, an explicit Quranic joining of iman and safety.
The section says the root sense of security is tranquility and fear's departure; here believing hearts find tranquility (تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ) in God's remembrance.
Ibrahim says he believes but asks to see the raising of birds “so my heart may be at rest”; the verse makes faith and settled assurance coexist, as the section's account of iman and security does.
During danger, God sends believers sleep as security, rain, and firmness for their hearts and feet; this concrete scene shows fear being removed and inward and bodily steadiness restored.
The section's title joins a trusted word to a settled heart; here God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in worldly life and the Hereafter, directly coupling belief with steadfastness.
This verse says God sent tranquility into believers' hearts so their faith would increase; it makes the section's link between faith and a calm, secure heart explicit.
After the pledge beneath the tree, God sends tranquility into the believers' hearts; the named inward settling follows a concrete act of allegiance and trust.

Those who say “our Lord is God” and then stand firm receive angels' reassurance not to fear or grieve and the promise of Paradise; this is the section's stable trust and fear removed in a single scene.
The angels continue by saying they are believers' protectors in worldly life and the Hereafter; this completes the reassurance begun in 41:30 with protection across both lives.
The angels identify this reassurance as hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful One, completing the promised welcome that follows the firm confession in 41:30.
When the wavering worshipper in 22:11 turns, this verse says he calls on what can neither harm nor benefit him; that ineffective refuge completes the consequence of unstable trust.
The continuation calls that invoked object a harmful patron and companion; it shows where the unstable reliance of 22:11–12 leads, not merely that the person changes stance.
After calling Moses back and assuring him in 28:31, God gives him two signs and tells him to go to Pharaoh; the secure return becomes a commission rather than continued retreat.

The section notes that messengers who call themselves trustworthy are answered with denial; this passage says Noah's people denied the messengers, the rejection that frames his “trustworthy messenger” claim in 26:107.
The section names emīn as trustworthy; Noah tells his people إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ, so the precise title is used by the messenger whose warning is under dispute.
Hud repeats the section's exact title رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ to his people, identifying himself as a trustworthy carrier before urging them to fear God and obey in the next verse.
Salih uses the same “trustworthy messenger” wording رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ; the repeated self-description shows that reliability is attached to the messenger's call, not a claim unique to Noah.
Lot likewise calls himself رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ before warning his people; this is another direct occurrence of the section's messenger-trust formulation.
Shuayb uses the same exact title رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ before telling his people to fear God and obey him, completing the repeated messenger pattern the section describes.

The section identifies the Spirit as a trustworthy carrier of revelation; this immediately preceding verse names the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, the source that 26:193's carrier conveys.
The section explicitly cites نَزَلَ بِهِ الرُّوحُ الْأَمِينُ: the trustworthy Spirit brings revelation, giving the divine message a reliable bearer.
The next verse says the revelation came down upon Muhammad's heart so he would be among the warners; it completes the passage's path from trustworthy carrier to receiving heart.
The section cites the carrier as obedient and trustworthy in 81:21; this passage first identifies the message as brought by a noble messenger, establishing who bears it.
The continuation describes that messenger as powerful and established near the Lord of the Throne; it gives the standing of the carrier called trustworthy in 81:21.
The section directly cites مُطَاعٍ ثَمَّ أَمِينٍ: the messenger is obeyed there and trustworthy, a precise description of faithful transmission.
This verse says the messenger is not withholding the unseen; it adds a specific mark of disclosure to the trustworthiness stated in 81:21.

The section's dictionary note reads the divine name al-Muʾmin as the One who makes good His promise to His servant; this verse names God الْمُؤْمِنُ among His attributes, placing that assurance in the Quran's own divine-name list.
The section glosses al-Muʾmin as the One who fulfills His promise; this verse says Satan promises people but gives them only delusion, a direct contrary promise.
Ibrahim asks God to make this place بَلَدًا آمِنًا and provide its people; the verse gives the secure city named in 95:3 a concrete prayer and provision context.
Ibrahim again asks that Mecca be made بَلَدًا آمِنًا; this is a direct parallel to the section's “secure city” and locates security in a prayer to God.
This oath opens with “this city” (بِهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ), the same city wording as 95:3; it places the surah's secure city inside a wider Quranic address to the city itself.
The next oath says the Prophet is dwelling in this city; it adds the Messenger's presence to the city's scene named in 90:1, alongside 95:3's “secure city.”
The sanctuary is a clear sign and whoever enters it is safe (آمِنًا); this ties the section's secure-city image to the Kaaba and its protected entry.
God says He made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a standing support for people; this gives the “secure city” image a concrete sanctuary at its center.

This verse contrasts the secure sanctuary God made for Mecca with people being snatched away around it, yet its residents believe falsehood and deny God's favor; safety does not itself ensure truthful faith.

The section's city is al-amīn, secure; this verse describes a town that was safe and settled (آمِنَةً مُّطْمَئِنَّةً) but lost that state through ingratitude, a specific reversal of security into fear and hunger.
God is said to have fed the Quraysh against hunger and made them safe from fear (وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ); it states the fear-removing sense that the section gives to ء م ن.
The promised return to the Sacred Mosque is explicitly “in safety” (آمِنِينَ); this connects secure entry into Mecca with the section's city and its assurance of safety.

The section explicitly cites إبراهيم's وَتَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا; its dictionary gloss for خ ل ق describes fabricating and shaping a lie in the mind, so this verse is the exact false-making claim set against God's creation.

Ibrahim's next words say that if they deny him, earlier peoples denied messengers too and the messenger's duty is clear delivery; this joins the fabricated claim in 29:17 to rejection of a trusted speaker.

After the verse about fabricating falsehood, Ibrahim asks whether people have not seen how God begins creation then repeats it; the passage directly distinguishes divine making from human fabrication.
The next verse tells people to travel the earth and observe how creation began; it develops the reality of God's making that stands against the fabricated objects and claims in 29:17–19.
The section explicitly quotes the deniers' claim إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا اخْتِلَاقٌ about revelation; this is a direct accusation that the true message is an invention.
The next verse shows their objection more specifically: why was the Reminder sent down to him from among them? It completes the social challenge behind calling revelation fabricated in 38:7.
This verse puts the two sides of the section's question together: who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies His signs? It names both fabrication and rejection of truth.

The same paired charge—fabricating about God or denying His signs—appears here, with the verse adding that such wrongdoers do not succeed; it makes the section's true-making/false-making contrast consequential.
This verse names those who invent a lie against God or deny His signs, then says the angels take their souls; the false claim is placed within an eventual reckoning.

This verse asks who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies the truth when it reaches him; that is the section's distinction between fabricated accusation and genuine revelation.
The verse again joins lying about God with denying truth when it comes, then asks whether Hell is not the disbelievers' home; it connects the section's fabrication/denial contrast to judgment.
Against the liar and denier named in 39:32, this verse describes the one who brings truth and the one who confirms it as God-conscious; it supplies the faithful response opposite to fabrication.

When opponents say the Prophet invented a lie about God, this verse answers that God blots out falsehood and establishes truth by His words, directly resolving the section's question about real making and invention.
This verse calls it a grave wrong to claim revelation falsely or to say “I will reveal like what God revealed”; it gives a concrete case of a human counterfeiting God's creative authority.
The claim that God revealed nothing to a human is answered by recalling the scripture given to Moses; the verse sets denial of revelation against a named, actual act of divine sending.

This verse describes people twisting their tongues so listeners think a statement belongs to Scripture when it does not, and attributing it to God; it is a specific word-made falsehood of the kind the section contrasts with true revelation.
The deniers call the Quran fabricated and are challenged to bring ten fabricated surahs like it; the challenge tests the very boundary between invented speech and revelation.
The continuation says that if they cannot answer, they should know the Quran was sent down with God's knowledge; it supplies the true source against the fabrication accusation in 11:13.
When a revelation is substituted for another, opponents say “you are only a fabricator”; this is the section's exact pattern of accusing a truthful messenger of invention.
The reply says the Holy Spirit brought revelation down in truth to make believers firm; this directly answers the accusation in 16:101 and links trusted transmission with firmness.

The next objection is that a human teaches the Prophet; the verse answers that the alleged teacher's language is foreign while the Quran is clear Arabic, giving the concrete basis of the dispute over its source.
The verse says those who invent falsehood are the ones who do not believe God's signs; it reverses the deniers' charge and identifies fabrication with their own lack of faith.

The companions of the cave say their people have taken other gods and ask for clear authority; “who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God?” makes fabricated worship claims a specific case of false making.
Opponents say the Quran is only a lie the Prophet invented and that others helped him; this directly stages the accusation of fabricated revelation named by the section.
They specify that the supposed invention is old tales written down and recited; the verse gives a concrete form to the accusation in 25:4.
The answer says the Quran was sent down by the One who knows the secret of the heavens and earth; this is the true source set against the fabrication claim of 25:4–5.
The opponents mock the claim that people will be created anew after disintegration; this is the resurrection dispute to which the next verse's accusation of invention responds.
The opponents call the warning either a lie invented against God or madness; the verse directly combines fabricated speech with the coming claim of resurrection.
The next verse asks whether they do not see what lies before and behind them of heaven and earth; it answers the mockery of renewed creation in 34:7 with visible created reality.
When clear signs are recited, the disbelievers call the message “nothing but a fabricated lie”; this is another direct rejection of a true message as invention.
Asked whether the Prophet invented the message, the answer says that if he had, no one could protect him from God; the accusation is placed under the judgment of the One who knows and witnesses.
The opponents say the Prophet has invented the Quran; this is a direct instance of the false-making charge developed in the section.
The next verse challenges them to produce a statement like it if they are truthful, testing the invented-speech claim rather than leaving it as a shared accusation.

Immediately after the challenge, the Quran asks whether they were created from nothing or are themselves creators; this makes the section's question about God's actual creation versus a fabricated claim explicit.
The next question asks whether they created the heavens and earth; it extends 52:35's creator question from human beings to the world that witnesses to its Maker.
The Quran says that even if humans and jinn gathered to produce its like, they could not; this gives a concrete test of the claim that revelation is merely manufactured speech.
The section cites the trustworthy carrier of revelation; this verse says the Quran is not the word of an expelled devil, a specific boundary against false attribution.
The continuation says God would cut the Messenger's aorta if he fabricated words; it completes the boundary stated in 69:44 with the stated consequence.
The next verse says none of them could prevent that consequence; it closes the passage's proof that the Messenger does not invent speech about God.
The section explicitly cites أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ; this verse asks the reader to look at the one who denies the dīn, the very denial the section puts opposite trust and belief.
The next verse identifies the denier by his act of repelling the orphan, showing how denial of the dīn appears in treatment of another person.
The continuation adds that he does not urge feeding the poor; it completes the practical description of the denier begun in 107:1–2.
The section cites the deniers of the Day of Judgment among people who cheat in measure; this opening woe introduces those traders, whose conduct 83:11 explicitly links to denying that Day.
The trader demands a full measure when taking for himself; this is one side of the specific cheating scene that the section connects to denial of judgment.
When measuring or weighing for others, the trader gives less; this completes the asymmetry in the fraud scene before 83:11 names denial of the Day.
The section explicitly cites الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ about those who cheat in measure; this verse names their denial of the Day of Judgment.
On the Day of judgment, the deniers are told “this is what you used to deny”; it completes the contrast between their earlier denial in 83:11 and the judgment they face.
The section quotes the people of Hell saying وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ; here they confess that denying the Day of Judgment was among the reasons they entered Saqar.
The next confession says they persisted until certainty came; it completes the admission in 74:46 by naming what ended their period of denial.
The section explicitly cites the question about one who كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, denies and turns away; this verse gives that paired action as the challenge to the one preventing prayer.
The next verse asks whether he does not know that God sees; it completes the denial-and-turning-away scene with the awareness of divine witness.
These people say there is only worldly life and deny being raised after death; this is a concrete rejection of the judgment and return whose denial the section asks what could justify.
When God's signs are recited, their only argument is to demand that their fathers be brought back if they are truthful; it makes their refusal of resurrection a challenge to the message.
The answer says God gives life and causes death, then gathers people for the Day of Resurrection; it supplies the divine power and appointed judgment denied in 45:24–25.
The section asks how people can deny the dīn after being created; this passage asks whether a human thinks he will be left without purpose or accountability.
The next verse recalls the human's beginning as a drop of semen; it provides the created origin behind the question about being left unaccountable.
The next step is that God made the drop into a clot, then created and proportioned it; this is a specific creation sequence that answers the section's claim about the human's made form.
The continuation says God made from it the two sexes, completing the account of bodily creation that leads to the question about resurrection.
The passage concludes by asking whether the One who did this can revive the dead; like the section's challenge after human creation, it connects making with the coming judgment.
The verse reminds humans that God created them from a drop, then notes that they become open disputants; it joins actual creation to the very posture of denial challenged in the section.
A man asks who can revive bones after they have crumbled; this is a direct denial of resurrection following the dispute about human creation.
The answer is that the One who originated them the first time will revive them; it grounds resurrection in the real creation that the section contrasts with fabricated claims.
The next argument asks whether the One who created the heavens and earth cannot create people like them; it extends the first-creation proof from bones to the whole world.
God's command when He wills a thing is only to say “Be,” and it is; this states how the Creator's act differs from human verbal invention.
The surah closes by declaring sovereignty belongs to the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things and to whom people return; this completes the creation-and-accountability argument.
The Quran describes human creation from an essence of clay; the section's question of actual divine creation versus fabrication has a concrete account of the human's origin.
The next verse places the human seed in a secure resting place; it adds the protected beginning of the bodily process described in 23:12–14.
The verse follows the stages of formation and calls God the best of creators; it directly supports the section's image of the human made in excellent form.
After detailing creation, the next verse says humans will die; it begins the passage's movement from created life toward the return relevant to the section's question about dīn.
The continuation says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, completing the creation, death, and judgment sequence.
The deniers' doubt about renewed creation is met by the question whether the first creation wearied God; this directly uses original making to answer denial of a new creation.
God begins creation and then repeats it, and people will be returned to Him; this joins true creation, return, and judgment in the order the section's verses set out.
The verse calls God's promise true, says all return to Him, and says He begins creation then repeats it; it binds fulfilled promise and divine making to the reckoning denied in the section.

After death, people are returned to God, their true Master, for judgment; the section's root gloss for ر د د includes returning and its dīn gloss concerns trust in judgment, which this verse brings together.

At the gathering, every soul is returned to God, its true Master, and the false objects it invoked disappear; this is a specific return for judgment that answers the section's wavering reliance and dīn theme.
The angel of death takes people and they are returned to their Lord; this literal return supplies a judgment scene for the section's repeated ر د د motif.

The verse says God gives life and then returns some people to the weakest age after knowledge; this is a specific bodily lowering that echoes 95:5's return to the lowest condition, though the two passages do not define that condition identically.

Whoever is given long life is reversed in creation, the verse says; this is a concrete bodily reversal relevant to 95:5's “returning” language, without requiring that the passages mean the same final state.
The address to the tranquil soul (النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ) directly echoes the section's dictionary account of security as calmness and fear gone.
The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord, pleased and pleasing; this joins the section's calm heart with its ر د د theme of return and its promise of reward.
The next verse welcomes the soul among God's servants; it develops the secure return of 89:28 into belonging among the faithful.
The final command is to enter Paradise; it completes the welcome and lasting reward that stand opposite the denial of dīn in the section.

The section's dictionary example of a lying cloth concerns an attractive surface that misrepresents its reality; this verse says the hypocrites' bodies impress and their speech draws listeners, yet compares them to propped-up timber, a specific outward/inward mismatch.

The section's secondary dictionary entry for ل ي س pictures camels that stay by a water basin and do not leave; Salih's she-camel is assigned a known drinking day here, a specific but indirect water-and-camel echo.

The section's secondary entry for ل ي س is the camel that stays at the trough; this nearby account divides the water between the people and the she-camel, a plausible but uncertain echo of that dictionary scene.

The section defines amānah as trustworthiness against betrayal; here the cosmic trust is offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, then borne by the human, whom the verse calls unjust and ignorant, a boundary between receiving a trust and proving reliable in it.

The section's dictionary gloss for ر د د describes repeated going and returning, and its gloss for ب ل د describes bewildered wavering; this verse says doubtful hearts “waver” (يَتَرَدَّدُونَ) within doubt, the direct opposite of settled trust.
The section opposes a settled heart to wavering trust; this person worships God at the edge, feels reassured when good comes, but turns back when tested, an explicit reversal of stable faith.

The section's secondary dictionary gloss for ك ذ ب describes a wild creature running and stopping to look behind; Moses here turns in flight and does not look back, then is called “approach, and do not fear” and told he is among the secure, reversing flight into safety.
At judgment, Satan admits “I promised you, then failed you” while God's promise was true; this reverses the section's description of Allah as al-Muʾmin, the fulfiller of His promise.

The section asks which making is real and which is fabricated; here God sets an absolute boundary, saying that if the Messenger had fabricated words against Him, He would seize him, so revelation cannot be treated as a human invention.
